planting.note: Set rooted divisions or cuttings into moist, fertile soil after the last frost; mint cultivars do not come true from seed, so propagation is always vegetative.

directions: Black Mitcham is the historic English-origin peppermint strain that became the backbone of American commercial peppermint oil production in the Pacific Northwest, prized for its exceptionally high menthol content and clean, intense peppermint flavor. Stems and leaf undersides carry a distinctive dark bronze-red flush that darkens further in cool weather, making the plant easy to distinguish from ordinary green peppermint at a glance. Grow it in a contained bed or sunken pot in consistently moist, rich soil, since like all mints it spreads aggressively by rhizome and will overrun neighboring plants if left unchecked. Choose this cultivar over generic peppermint when you want the strongest, most classic peppermint flavor for tea, extracts, or candy-making.

planting.note: Plant divisions or rooted cuttings after last frost in moist, fertile soil; this cultivar is propagated vegetatively since variegation does not come true from seed.

directions: Golden Ginger Mint is a variegated selection of the naturally occurring spearmint x corn mint hybrid, its narrow, slightly wrinkled leaves streaked and edged in bright gold against dark green, giving it strong ornamental value beyond its warm, spicy-gingery aroma. The red-tinted stems and gold-splashed foliage make it easy to identify in a mixed herb bed even before you brush a leaf to release its scent. Grow it in part shade to prevent the variegation from scorching in hot afternoon sun, and confine the roots in a buried container since it spreads by runners just as vigorously as any other mint. Use the leaves fresh in iced tea, fruit salads, or Southeast Asian-style dishes where a ginger note complements mint's natural coolness.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Start seed indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost, then transplant once soil is reliably warm; this dwarf French cultivar also thrives sown directly into a windowsill pot.

directions: Marseillais is a traditional dwarf French basil that packs classic, intensely essence-of-basil flavor into a tight, mounded 8-10 inch plant, making it one of the most space-efficient basils for a kitchen windowsill or small container. Its leaves are proportionately large for such a compact plant, and the dense branching habit means frequent light harvesting keeps it productive for months rather than bolting quickly like larger basils. Pinch the growing tips regularly once the plant reaches 4-6 inches to encourage the bushy, rounded form that gives this cultivar its French market-garden reputation. Choose it over Genovese-type basils when growing space is limited but full basil flavor is still the goal.

planting.note: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost and transplant into warm, fertile soil once frost danger has fully passed.

directions: Superbo is an Italian-bred Genovese-type basil selected specifically for plant-to-plant uniformity, giving growers a medium-compact, evenly sized crop that is easier to manage than open-pollinated Genovese strains. The broad, spoon-shaped leaves are a brilliant deep green and hold their glossy sheen and flavor well after cutting, which is why this cultivar became a standard for commercial bunching and pesto processing in Italy. Pinch flower spikes as they appear to extend the harvest window and prevent the leaves from turning bitter. Grow it side by side with a standard Genovese basil if you want to compare uniformity and leaf shape, since the two share nearly identical flavor profiles.
sources: Rutgers New Jersey Agricultural Experiment Station

planting.note: Start seed indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost and transplant into full sun once soil has warmed thoroughly.

directions: Persian Basil, a 2015 All-America Selections winner, produces large, soft silvery-green leaves with an assertive spicy flavor combining clove, anise, and a hint of lemon that sets it apart from sweeter Genovese-type basils. The sturdy, upright plants are notably slow to bolt, holding good flavor and tender texture well into summer while many other basils turn bitter once they flower. It is the traditional basil of Persian cuisine, eaten fresh as part of sabzi khordan herb platters and stirred into stews, rice dishes, and grilled meats. Give it full sun and steady moisture, and harvest by pinching stem tips regularly to keep the plant bushy and delay flowering even longer.
